title: Lecture 3 — Functions, Modularity, and Version Control
text:
10.1 Why test functions?
Testing ensures:

Functions produce correct results
Changes don’t break existing functionality
Edge cases are handled properly
Code behaves as documented


def calculate_mean_test(values):
    """Calculate arithmetic mean."""
    return sum(values) / len(values)

# Test with known values
assert calculate_mean_test([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) == 3.0
assert calculate_mean_test([10, 20]) == 15.0
assert calculate_mean_test([5]) == 5.0

print("All tests passed!")

All tests passed!

title: Lecture 3 — Functions, Modularity, and Version Control
text:
10.2 Types of tests
Unit tests: Test individual functions in isolation

def calculate_return_func(initial, final):
    """Calculate simple return."""
    return (final - initial) / initial

def test_calculate_return():
    """Test return calculation."""
    # Basic case
    assert calculate_return_func(100, 110) == 0.10
    
    # Loss case
    assert calculate_return_func(100, 90) == -0.10
    
    # No change
    assert calculate_return_func(100, 100) == 0.0
    
    print("Return calculation tests passed!")

test_calculate_return()

Return calculation tests passed!


Edge case tests: Test boundary conditions

def test_edge_cases():
    """Test edge cases for mean calculation."""
    # Single value
    assert calculate_mean_test([5]) == 5.0
    
    # Negative values
    assert calculate_mean_test([-1, -2, -3]) == -2.0
    
    # Mixed signs
    assert calculate_mean_test([-1, 0, 1]) == 0.0
    
    print("Edge case tests passed!")

test_edge_cases()

Edge case tests passed!

title: Lecture 3 — Functions, Modularity, and Version Control
text:
11.1 Single Responsibility Principle
Each function should do one thing well:
Bad:

def analyze_data(data):
    """Do everything (too much!)."""
    # Clean data
    cleaned = [x for x in data if x is not None]
    
    # Calculate statistics
    mean = sum(cleaned) / len(cleaned)
    variance = sum((x - mean)**2 for x in cleaned) / len(cleaned)
    
    # Generate report
    print(f"Mean: {mean}")
    print(f"Variance: {variance}")
    
    # Save to file
    with open('results.txt', 'w') as f:
        f.write(f"{mean},{variance}\n")
    
    return mean, variance

Good:

def clean_data(data):
    """Remove None values."""
    return [x for x in data if x is not None]

def calculate_statistics_func(data):
    """Calculate mean and variance."""
    mean = sum(data) / len(data)
    variance = sum((x - mean)**2 for x in data) / len(data)
    return mean, variance

def print_statistics(mean, variance):
    """Print statistics."""
    print(f"Mean: {mean}")
    print(f"Variance: {variance}")

# Main workflow is now clear
data_example = [1, 2, None, 3, 4]
cleaned = clean_data(data_example)
mean_val, var_val = calculate_statistics_func(cleaned)
print_statistics(mean_val, var_val)

Mean: 2.5
Variance: 1.25

title: Lecture 3 — Functions, Modularity, and Version Control
text:
11.2 Clear naming
Function names should clearly indicate purpose:
Good names:

calculate_mean()
filter_positive_values()
convert_to_returns()
validate_inputs()

Poor names:

do_stuff()
process()
calc()
func1()

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
These notes provide a systematic reference for the material introduced in Lecture 8’s class.qmd and class.R. The central theme of this lecture is a translation, not a reinvention: everything you already know about computation from seven lectures of Python – variables, collections, control flow, functions, vectorization, and reproducible workflows – continues to apply. What changes is notation, a handful of default behaviors, and, in some places, which idiom experienced users prefer.
R was created in 1993 by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman as a free implementation of the S language, itself designed at Bell Labs for statistical computing. Python was created slightly earlier, in 1991, by Guido van Rossum as a general-purpose scripting language; its scientific capabilities (NumPy, pandas, SciPy) were added over the following two decades by the open-source community. This history explains a great deal about why the two languages feel different in practice:

R treats vectors and data frames as native, built-in concepts. There is no equivalent of “importing NumPy” to get vectorized arithmetic; it is simply how R works.
Python treats collections as a general-purpose list, with vectorized numerical behavior available only once you import NumPy.
R’s standard library is comparatively small; most functionality (plotting, data wrangling, modeling extensions) comes from packages on CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network.
Python’s standard library is larger, but the scientific stack is still delivered via third-party packages (NumPy, pandas, matplotlib) in a similar fashion.

Both languages are dynamically typed, both support functions as first-class objects, both have mechanisms for iteration and vectorized operations, and both can be used interactively or as scripts. The remainder of these notes works through the specific syntax and idioms you need to translate your existing computational fluency from Python into R.






NoteA Note on Scope



This lecture (and these notes) cover base R – the functionality available without loading any packages beyond what ships with R itself. Lecture 9 introduces the tidyverse, a separate ecosystem of packages that provides a more modern, consistent grammar for data manipulation. Everything in this lecture remains useful once you start using the tidyverse; in fact, many tidyverse functions are thin, more readable wrappers around base R operations you will learn today.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
2.1 Two Modes of Use
Exactly as with Python, R supports two primary modes of interaction:
Interactive mode: you type commands one at a time at the > prompt (in a terminal, or in RStudio’s Console pane) and see results immediately. This is ideal for exploration, debugging, and quick calculations.
Script mode: you save a sequence of commands in a .R file and execute the whole file at once, either with Rscript filename.R from the command line, or by clicking “Source” in RStudio, or line-by-line with Ctrl+Enter.

# This line runs identically whether typed interactively or sourced from a script
x <- 10
x

[1] 10

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
2.2 Objects
R documentation almost universally refers to “objects” rather than “variables.” The term is used broadly: numbers, vectors, data frames, functions, and even plots are all objects in R, each with a class that determines how generic functions (like print() or summary()) behave on them. This is conceptually similar to how “everything is an object” in Python, including functions and modules.

x <- 10
class(x)

[1] "numeric"

f <- function(x) x^2
class(f)

[1] "function"

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
2.3 Functions
Functions in R are called with parentheses, just as in Python: mean(x), sqrt(16), print("hello"). R has an enormous number of built-in and package-provided functions; discovering the right function for a task is a large part of learning R fluently.

sqrt(16)

[1] 4

round(3.14159, 2)

[1] 3.14

nchar("hello")  # analogous to Python's len("hello")

[1] 5

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
2.4 Packages and the R Ecosystem
A package in R bundles functions, data, and documentation together, just as a Python package (installed via pip) does. R’s package repository is called CRAN. Installing and loading a package uses two separate steps:

install.packages("dplyr")  # done once, like pip install
library(dplyr)              # done each session, like import

This differs slightly from Python’s import statement, which handles both “the package must already be installed” and “load it into this session” implicitly (Python raises an error if the package was never installed; R’s install.packages() and library() are explicitly separate steps).






TipChecking Installed Packages



Use installed.packages() to list everything installed, or library() with no arguments to open a package browser in RStudio. To check whether a specific package is already available without loading it, use requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE).

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
section: 2.5 R versus Python: A Summary of Design Philosophy
text:
2.5 R versus Python: A Summary of Design Philosophy








Aspect
Python
R




Origin
General-purpose scripting language
Statistical computing language (descended from S)


Native numeric collection
list (not vectorized)
vector (vectorized by default)


Scientific stack
Third-party (NumPy, pandas, SciPy)
Largely native, extended by tidyverse


Typical community
Software engineering, data science, scripting
Statistics, biostatistics, econometrics, academic research


Package repository
PyPI
CRAN


Indexing
0-based
1-based


Assignment operator
=
<- (idiomatic), = also works

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
3.1 Variables / Objects
Python:
x = 10
R:

x <- 10

Both <- and = work for assignment at the top level in R, but <- is the idiomatic choice, and some contexts (such as naming arguments inside a function call) require = specifically, which can create ambiguity if you use = for assignment everywhere. We will consistently use <- for assignment and reserve = for passing named arguments.

# <- for assignment, = for naming an argument
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14








TipKeyboard Shortcut



RStudio provides a keyboard shortcut for typing <-: Alt + - (Windows/Linux) or Option + - (Mac). Learning this shortcut early will save you a great deal of typing.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
3.2 Python Lists/Arrays <-> R Vectors
A Python list is a general-purpose ordered collection that can hold mixed types without complaint. A NumPy array is homogeneous and supports vectorized arithmetic. R’s vector, created with c(), behaves like the NumPy array: homogeneous (R will silently coerce mixed types to a common type) and vectorized by default.

# R vector: homogeneous, vectorized
v <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
v * 2

[1] 2 4 6 8



# Mixing types in c() triggers coercion, not an error
mixed <- c(1, 2, "three")
mixed       # everything became character

[1] "1"     "2"     "three"

class(mixed)

[1] "character"








ImportantSilent Coercion Is a Common Source of Bugs



Unlike Python, which raises a TypeError if you try to add a number and a string, R’s c() will silently coerce all elements to the most general type present (logical -> integer -> double -> character, in that order). Always check class() on a vector if its behavior surprises you.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
3.3 NumPy Arrays <-> R Vectorized Operations
Both NumPy and R allow you to apply an operation to every element of a collection without writing an explicit loop.
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
arr + 10

v <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
v + 10

[1] 11 12 13 14


The key practical difference: in Python, you must deliberately choose to use NumPy to get this behavior (plain lists do not vectorize). In R, there is no “plain list” numeric type to fall back to – vectors are vectorized unconditionally.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
3.4 pandas DataFrames <-> Data Frames / Tibbles
pandas’ DataFrame was explicitly inspired by R’s data frame; the resemblance is intentional, not coincidental.
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Ada", "Grace"], "score": [92, 88]})

df <- data.frame(name = c("Ada", "Grace"), score = c(92, 88))
df

   name score
1   Ada    92
2 Grace    88


A tibble (from the tidyverse, covered in Lecture 9) is a modernized data frame with more predictable printing and fewer surprising default behaviors. For today, base data.frame() is sufficient.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
section: 3.6 Python Boolean Indexing <-> R Logical Filtering
text:
3.6 Python Boolean Indexing <-> R Logical Filtering
import numpy as np
scores = np.array([85, 92, 78, 95])
scores[scores > 90]

scores <- c(85, 92, 78, 95)
scores[scores > 90]

[1] 92 95


The underlying mechanism is identical in spirit: a logical/boolean vector of the same length as the data is used to select elements where the value is TRUE.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
4.1 The Four Core Types
R has four atomic vector types used constantly in everyday work:

class(TRUE)     # logical

[1] "logical"

class(5L)       # integer

[1] "integer"

class(5.0)      # double (R calls this "numeric")

[1] "numeric"

class("hello")  # character

[1] "character"





R type
Python analogue
Literal syntax in R




logical
bool
TRUE, FALSE (or T, F)


integer
int
5L (the L suffix forces an integer)


double / numeric
float
5.0 or simply 5


character
str
"hello" or 'hello'









NoteWhy Does 5 Default to Double, Not Integer?



In R, a bare numeric literal like 5 is stored as a double by default, not an integer. This differs from some other languages. If you specifically need an integer (rare in everyday data analysis), append L: 5L. In practice, the distinction between integer and double rarely matters for day-to-day analysis, since R’s arithmetic functions happily operate on both.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
4.2 Case Sensitivity and Logical Literals
R is case-sensitive, just like Python. TRUE and FALSE must be spelled with the exact capitalization shown; true, True, and false will all raise errors (R does not define them). The shorthand T and F exist but are discouraged in careful code, since T and F are ordinary variable names that could be reassigned, unlike the protected keywords TRUE/FALSE.

x <- true  # Error: object 'true' not found

Error:
! object 'true' not found



T <- 5          # legal but dangerous -- T no longer means TRUE!
if (T) {
  print("this won't print, because T is now 5, not TRUE... actually 5 is truthy")
}

[1] "this won't print, because T is now 5, not TRUE... actually 5 is truthy"

T <- TRUE  # restore sanity

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
4.3 Type Coercion Hierarchy
When R combines mixed types in a single vector via c(), it coerces everything to the most general type present, following this order (least to most general):
logical -> integer -> double -> character

c(TRUE, 1L)        # integer vector: TRUE becomes 1L

[1] 1 1

c(TRUE, 1.5)       # double vector: TRUE becomes 1.0

[1] 1.0 1.5

c(1, "a")          # character vector: 1 becomes "1"

[1] "1" "a"

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
4.4 Checking and Converting Types
Analogous to Python’s isinstance() and explicit casting (int(x), str(x)), R provides is.*() checks and as.*() conversions.

is.numeric(5)

[1] TRUE

is.character("hello")

[1] TRUE

is.logical(TRUE)

[1] TRUE



as.character(5)

[1] "5"

as.numeric("3.14")

[1] 3.14

as.integer(3.99)  # truncates toward zero, like Python's int()

[1] 3



as.numeric("abc")  # produces NA with a warning, not an error

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion


[1] NA








ImportantFailed Conversions Produce NA, Not an Error



Where Python’s int("abc") raises a ValueError, R’s as.numeric("abc") returns NA and issues a warning rather than stopping execution. This means a bad conversion can silently propagate through your analysis if you are not checking for NA values afterward.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
6.1 Lists as R’s General-Purpose Container
Where an R vector must be homogeneous, an R list() can hold elements of different types, different lengths, and can be named – similar in spirit to a Python dict, though R lists also preserve order like a Python list.

person <- list(name = "Ada", age = 36, languages = c("R", "Python"))
person

$name
[1] "Ada"

$age
[1] 36

$languages
[1] "R"      "Python"

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
6.2 Accessing List Elements
R provides three related-but-different extraction operators, which trip up many newcomers:

person$name        # by name, returns the unwrapped value

[1] "Ada"

person[["name"]]    # by name or position, returns the unwrapped value

[1] "Ada"

person["name"]      # by name or position, returns a sub-list (still a list!)

$name
[1] "Ada"



class(person$name)    # character

[1] "character"

class(person["name"])  # list

[1] "list"








ImportantSingle Brackets vs. Double Brackets



[[ ]] extracts the actual contents (an R analogue of a Python dictionary’s d["key"]). A single [ ] on a list returns a smaller list containing that element, not the element itself. This distinction has no Python analogue and is one of the most common sources of confusion for newcomers. As a rule of thumb: use [[ ]] or $ when you want the value, and [ ] only when you deliberately want to keep working with a list.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
section: 6.3 Lists Can Nest and Hold Mixed Lengths
text:
6.3 Lists Can Nest and Hold Mixed Lengths

mixed_list <- list(
  numbers = c(1, 2, 3),
  label = "example",
  nested = list(a = 1, b = 2)
)
mixed_list$nested$a

[1] 1

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
7.1 Creating a Data Frame

df <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ada", "Grace", "Alan"),
  score = c(92, 88, 95)
)
df

   name score
1   Ada    92
2 Grace    88
3  Alan    95


A data frame is, structurally, a list of equal-length vectors, displayed as a table. Each column is a vector (so each column must be internally homogeneous), but different columns can hold different types – exactly like a pandas DataFrame or an R list where every element happens to be the same length.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
7.2 Inspecting a Data Frame

str(df)      # structure: types and a preview of each column

'data.frame':   3 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ name : chr  "Ada" "Grace" "Alan"
 $ score: num  92 88 95

summary(df)  # summary statistics for each column

     name               score      
 Length:3           Min.   :88.00  
 Class :character   1st Qu.:90.00  
 Mode  :character   Median :92.00  
                    Mean   :91.67  
                    3rd Qu.:93.50  
                    Max.   :95.00  

nrow(df)

[1] 3

ncol(df)

[1] 2

dim(df)

[1] 3 2

colnames(df)

[1] "name"  "score"

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
7.3 Accessing Columns and Rows

df$score          # column, by name, as a vector (most common)

[1] 92 88 95

df[["score"]]      # equivalent to df$score

[1] 92 88 95

df[, "score"]      # equivalent, using bracket notation with a comma

[1] 92 88 95

df[1, ]            # first row, all columns

  name score
1  Ada    92

df[1, "score"]     # first row, score column only

[1] 92








NoteThe Comma Inside Brackets



R’s data frame bracket syntax is df[rows, columns]. Leaving one side blank means “all.” df[1, ] means “row 1, all columns.” df[, "score"] means “all rows, the score column.” This comma-separated syntax has no direct single-bracket equivalent in pandas, where .loc[] and .iloc[] are used instead, but the underlying idea (specify a row selector and a column selector) is the same.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
7.4 Logical Filtering of Rows

df[df$score > 90, ]

  name score
1  Ada    92
3 Alan    95


This reads as: “Take the rows where the logical condition df$score > 90 is TRUE, and all columns.” It is the direct structural analogue of pandas’ df[df["score"] > 90].

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
7.5 Adding and Modifying Columns

df$passed <- df$score >= 90
df

   name score passed
1   Ada    92   TRUE
2 Grace    88  FALSE
3  Alan    95   TRUE

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
7.6 data.frame() versus tibble()
Base R’s data.frame() has a handful of quirky default behaviors (recycling columns of mismatched length with a warning rather than an error, printing all rows by default even for huge tables, and historically auto-converting strings to factors). The tidyverse’s tibble(), introduced properly in Lecture 9, addresses these quirks with more predictable defaults. We use data.frame() today because it requires no additional packages, but expect the transition to tibbles next lecture to feel almost seamless.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
8.1 NA Is Typed
Unlike Python’s single universal None, R’s NA comes in several typed flavors (NA as logical, NA_integer_, NA_real_, NA_character_), though in practice R converts between these automatically and you rarely need to worry about the distinction.

x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
is.na(x)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
8.2 NA Propagation

sum(x)                 # NA

[1] NA

sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)    # 7

[1] 7

mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 2.333333








ImportantCompare to Python’s None



In Python, sum([1, 2, None, 4]) raises a TypeError immediately. In R, sum() silently returns NA rather than erroring. This “fail silently” behavior means you must proactively check is.na() or use na.rm = TRUE; R will not stop and complain for you.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
8.3 Removing or Replacing Missing Values

x[!is.na(x)]          # keep only non-missing values

[1] 1 2 4

ifelse(is.na(x), 0, x) # replace NA with 0, elementwise

[1] 1 2 0 4

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
9.2 Implicit Return Values

square_implicit <- function(x) {
  x^2  # the value of the last evaluated expression is returned automatically
}
square_implicit(5)

[1] 25


Many experienced R programmers omit return() for short, single-expression functions, relying on the implicit return. We will use explicit return() in the early part of the course for clarity, matching the style you are used to from Python, and relax this later.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
9.3 Default Arguments and Named Arguments

describe <- function(name, title = "Dr.") {
  paste(title, name)
}
describe("Smith")

[1] "Dr. Smith"

describe("Smith", title = "Prof.")

[1] "Prof. Smith"

describe(name = "Smith", title = "Prof.")

[1] "Prof. Smith"

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
9.4 Variable Numbers of Arguments
Python’s *args/**kwargs have a rough analogue in R’s ... (“dots”).

add_all <- function(...) {
  sum(...)
}
add_all(1, 2, 3, 4)

[1] 10

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
10.2 Reading (Not Modifying) an Outer Variable

counter_value <- 0

show_counter <- function() {
  print(counter_value)  # reading an outer variable is fine
}
show_counter()

[1] 0

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
10.3 The <<- Operator (Use Sparingly)
R has a “superassignment” operator <<- that modifies a variable in an enclosing scope rather than creating a new local variable. It is the rough analogue of Python’s global keyword, but can reach further up through nested function environments. It is rarely needed in everyday data analysis and is easy to misuse; we mention it here mainly so you recognize it when you see it in other people’s code.

counter_value <- 0

increment_global <- function() {
  counter_value <<- counter_value + 1
}
increment_global()
counter_value  # now 1

[1] 1








ImportantPrefer Return Values Over <<-



Just as in Python, where modifying global state from inside a function is discouraged in favor of returning a new value, R style strongly prefers functions that take inputs and return outputs, rather than functions that reach outside themselves to modify state via <<-. Treat <<- as a tool of last resort.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
11.1 for Loops

for (i in 1:5) {
  print(i^2)
}

[1] 1
[1] 4
[1] 9
[1] 16
[1] 25


R’s for loop iterates directly over the elements of a vector (or list), rather than requiring something like Python’s range().






Important1:5 Includes Both Endpoints



Python’s range(1, 5) produces 1, 2, 3, 4 (excludes the stop value). R’s 1:5 produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (includes both endpoints). This is one of the most common sources of off-by-one bugs when translating code between the languages.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
section: 11.2 Iterating Over Something Other Than a Numeric Sequence
text:
11.2 Iterating Over Something Other Than a Numeric Sequence

for (name in c("Ada", "Grace", "Alan")) {
  print(paste("Hello,", name))
}

[1] "Hello, Ada"
[1] "Hello, Grace"
[1] "Hello, Alan"

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
11.3 while Loops

n <- 1
while (n < 5) {
  print(n)
  n <- n + 1
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3
[1] 4


Structurally identical to Python’s while loop; the main difference is R’s curly-brace block syntax rather than Python’s indentation-based blocks.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
11.4 seq_along() for Safe Index Iteration

values <- c(10, 20, 30)
for (i in seq_along(values)) {
  print(values[i])
}

[1] 10
[1] 20
[1] 30


seq_along(values) is the safe way to generate indices 1:length(values); it correctly produces an empty sequence if values has length 0, whereas 1:length(values) would incorrectly produce 1:0, i.e., c(1, 0), and attempt two iterations on an empty vector. This parallels why Python programmers prefer for i, x in enumerate(values) or for x in values over manually indexing with range(len(values)).

empty <- c()
length(empty)

[1] 0

seq_along(empty)  # correctly empty

integer(0)

1:length(empty)   # incorrectly produces c(1, 0) -- a classic bug

[1] 1 0

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
section: 12.1 Why Loops Are Usually the Wrong Tool in R
text:
12.1 Why Loops Are Usually the Wrong Tool in R

values <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

# Loop version -- works, but is not idiomatic R
squared_loop <- numeric(length(values))
for (i in seq_along(values)) {
  squared_loop[i] <- values[i]^2
}
squared_loop

[1]  1  4  9 16 25



# Vectorized version -- idiomatic R
squared_vectorized <- values^2
squared_vectorized

[1]  1  4  9 16 25



identical(squared_loop, squared_vectorized)

[1] TRUE


In NumPy, vectorization is a performance option you choose by using arrays instead of lists. In R, essentially all arithmetic, comparison, and many string operations are vectorized by default on the language’s native vector type, and writing an explicit loop to perform elementwise arithmetic is both slower and considered poor style.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
12.2 Recycling
A subtlety with no clean Python analogue: when R performs vectorized arithmetic on vectors of different lengths, it recycles the shorter vector by repeating it.

c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)  # recycles c(10, 20) to c(10, 20, 10, 20)

[1] 11 22 13 24



c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20)  # length mismatch not a multiple -- warns, still runs

Warning in c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20): longer object length is not a multiple of
shorter object length


[1] 11 22 13








ImportantRecycling Can Hide Bugs



Recycling is sometimes useful (e.g., adding a single number to every element, which is recycling a length-1 vector), but recycling vectors of unrelated lengths without noticing is a real source of subtle bugs. Always check vector lengths with length() if an operation produces a surprising result.

title: Lecture 8 – Python to R: Two Languages, One Computational Model
text:
12.3 The apply Family (Conceptual Introduction)
When a vectorized arithmetic shortcut does not exist, or when applying a more complex function to every element, R’s apply family plays a role similar to Python’s map() or list comprehensions.

values <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
sapply(values, function(x) x^2)

[1]  1  4  9 16 25



# For a list, lapply() returns a list rather than attempting to simplify
lapply(list(1, "a", TRUE), class)

[[1]]
[1] "numeric"

[[2]]
[1] "character"

[[3]]
[1] "logical"











Function
Input
Output
Rough Python analogue




sapply()
vector or list
vector (simplified)
list comprehension / map() + conversion


lapply()
vector or list
list
map() (returns an iterator of results)


vapply()
vector or list
vector (with explicit type check)
list comprehension with type checking


mapply()
multiple vectors
vector/list
map() over multiple iterables (zip + map)









TipPreference Order



Prefer, in order: (1) a direct vectorized operation if one exists (values^2); (2) sapply()/lapply() if you need to apply a custom function elementwise; (3) an explicit for loop only when neither of the above is feasible (for example, when each iteration depends on the result of the previous one). This mirrors the Python hierarchy of preferring vectorized NumPy operations, then comprehensions/map(), then explicit loops.

title: Lecture 6: Testing, Debugging, and AI-Assisted Programming
text:
def calculate_mean_v1(values):
    """Calculate mean of values. Return None if empty."""
    return sum(values) / len(values)

def test_calculate_mean_single_value():
    """Test mean calculation with one value."""
    result = calculate_mean_v1([42])
    expected = 42.0
    assert result == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result}"
    print("Test passed: single value")

test_calculate_mean_single_value()

Test passed: single value


Instructor notes:
Students should recognize that a single-value list should return that value as the mean. Common mistakes include:

Forgetting to test edge cases at all
Not using descriptive test function names
Not including the assertion message for helpful debugging

Teaching tip: Have students predict what should happen before writing the test. Ask: “What should the mean of [42] be?” This reinforces thinking about requirements before coding.





def is_valid_temperature(temp):
    """
    Check if temperature is valid (between -50 and 150 Fahrenheit).
    
    Args:
        temp: numeric temperature value
        
    Returns:
        bool: True if valid, False otherwise
    """
    return -50 <= temp <= 150

# Test 1: Valid temperature
result = is_valid_temperature(72)
assert result == True, "72 F should be valid"
print("Test 1 passed: valid temperature")

# Test 2: Too cold
result = is_valid_temperature(-100)
assert result == False, "-100 F should be invalid"
print("Test 2 passed: too cold")

# Test 3: Too hot
result = is_valid_temperature(200)
assert result == False, "200 F should be invalid"
print("Test 3 passed: too hot")

Test 1 passed: valid temperature
Test 2 passed: too cold
Test 3 passed: too hot


Instructor notes:
This exercise reinforces the pattern of writing multiple tests for one function. Watch for:

Students testing only the “happy path” (valid case)
Students not testing both boundaries (too hot AND too cold)
Confusion about inclusive vs exclusive boundaries

Teaching tip: Ask “What other cases should we test?” Boundary values are crucial: exactly -50, exactly 150, slightly beyond boundaries.
Alternative implementation that students might write:

# Alternative: More explicit
def is_valid_temperature_v2(temp):
    if temp < -50:
        return False
    if temp > 150:
        return False
    return True

Both are correct. Discuss readability vs conciseness.





def remove_missing_values(values):
    """
    Remove None values from list.
    
    Args:
        values: list that may contain None
        
    Returns:
        list: values with None removed
    """
    return [v for v in values if v is not None]

# Test 1: Some None values
result = remove_missing_values([1, None, 3, None, 5])
expected = [1, 3, 5]
assert result == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result}"
print("Test 1 passed: some None values")

# Test 2: No None values
result = remove_missing_values([1, 2, 3])
expected = [1, 2, 3]
assert result == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result}"
print("Test 2 passed: no None values")

# Test 3: Only None values
result = remove_missing_values([None, None])
expected = []
assert result == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result}"
print("Test 3 passed: only None values")

# Test 4: Empty list
result = remove_missing_values([])
expected = []
assert result == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result}"
print("Test 4 passed: empty list")

Test 1 passed: some None values
Test 2 passed: no None values
Test 3 passed: only None values
Test 4 passed: empty list


Instructor notes:
This is a comprehensive test suite that covers all major scenarios. Students often forget:

The empty list case (simplest edge case)
The “all None” case (extreme edge case)
The “no None” case (another happy path)

Common mistake: Using == None instead of is None. Both work but is None is more Pythonic.
Alternative implementation using filter:

def remove_missing_values_v2(values):
    return list(filter(lambda x: x is not None, values))

Discuss readability: list comprehension is usually clearer.





def normalize_temperatures(temps):
    """
    Normalize temperatures to 0-1 scale using min-max normalization.
    Formula: (value - min) / (max - min)
    
    Args:
        temps: list of temperature values
        
    Returns:
        list: normalized values (0-1 scale)
    """
    if len(temps) == 0:
        return []
    
    min_temp = min(temps)
    max_temp = max(temps)
    
    # Handle case where all values are the same
    if max_temp == min_temp:
        return [0.5] * len(temps)  # or could return all 0s or all 1s
    
    return [(t - min_temp) / (max_temp - min_temp) for t in temps]

        f"At index {i}: expected {expected[i]}, got {result[i]}"
print("Test 1 passed: normal case")

# Test 2: All same value

# This is a design decision: what should happen?

def calculate_median_fixed(values):
    """
    Calculate median of values.
    
    Args:
        values: list of numeric values
        
    Returns:
        float: median value, or None if empty
    """
    if len(values) == 0:
        return None
    
    sorted_values = sorted(values)
    n = len(sorted_values)
    middle = n // 2  # Integer division!
    
    if n % 2 == 1:
        # Odd length: return middle element
        return sorted_values[middle]
    else:
        # Even length: return average of two middle elements
        return (sorted_values[middle - 1] + sorted_values[middle]) / 2

def get_temperature_range_fixed(temps):
    """
    Get range of temperatures (max - min).
    
    Args:
        temps: list of temperature values
        
    Returns:
        float: max - min, or None if empty
    """
    if len(temps) == 0:
        return None
    
    min_temp = temps[0]
    max_temp = temps[0]
    
    # Fix: Check ALL elements
    for i in range(len(temps)):
        if temps[i] < min_temp:
            min_temp = temps[i]
        if temps[i] > max_temp:
            max_temp = temps[i]
    
    return max_temp - min_temp

def calculate_total_rainfall_robust(daily_rain):
    """
    Sum daily rainfall, handling type mismatches gracefully.
    
    Args:
        daily_rain: list of rainfall measurements (should be numeric)
        
    Returns:
        float: total rainfall, skipping invalid values
    """
    total = 0
    for i, rain in enumerate(daily_rain):
        # Handle numeric types directly
        if isinstance(rain, (int, float)):
            total += rain
        # Try to convert strings
        elif isinstance(rain, str):
            try:
                converted = float(rain)
                total += converted
            except ValueError:
                print(f"Warning: Skipping invalid string at index {i}: '{rain}'")
        # Skip None
        elif rain is None:
            print(f"Warning: Skipping None at index {i}")
        # Unknown types
        else:
            print(f"Warning: Skipping unknown type at index {i}: {type(rain)}")
    
    return total

def calculate_std_dev(values):
    """Calculate standard deviation (sample)."""
    if len(values) == 0:
        return None
    if len(values) == 1:
        return 0.0  # Single value has no variation
    
    n = len(values)
    mean = sum(values) / n
    
    # Use n-1 for sample standard deviation
    variance = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in values) / (n - 1)
    return variance ** 0.5

def remove_outliers(values, z_threshold=2):
    """Remove outliers beyond z_threshold standard deviations."""
    if len(values) < 2:
        return values  # Can't calculate std dev with < 2 values
    
    mean = sum(values) / len(values)
    std_dev = calculate_std_dev(values)
    
    if std_dev == 0:
        # All values are the same -- no outliers
        return values
    
    return [x for x in values if abs(x - mean) <= z_threshold * std_dev]

def moving_average_corrected(values, window_size):
    """
    Calculate moving average, excluding incomplete windows.
    
    Args:
        values: list of numeric values
        window_size: size of moving window (must be >= 1)
        
    Returns:
        list: moving averages (length may be shorter than input)
    """
    # Handle edge cases
    if window_size < 1:
        raise ValueError("window_size must be >= 1")
    
    if len(values) < window_size:
        return []
    
    # Special case: window_size == 1
    if window_size == 1:
        return list(values)  # Return copy
    
    # Calculate moving averages for complete windows only
    result = []
    for i in range(len(values) - window_size + 1):
        window = values[i:i+window_size]
        avg = sum(window) / window_size
        result.append(avg)
    
    return result

def fill_with_mean_naive(temps):
    """Fill missing values with mean of valid values."""
    valid_temps = [t for t in temps if t is not None]
    if len(valid_temps) == 0:
        return temps  # All None, can't compute mean
    mean_temp = sum(valid_temps) / len(valid_temps)
    return [t if t is not None else mean_temp for t in temps]

def fill_forward(temps):
    """Fill missing values by carrying forward last valid value."""
    filled = []
    last_valid = None
    for temp in temps:
        if temp is not None:
            filled.append(temp)
            last_valid = temp
        else:
            # Use last valid value, or None if we haven't seen one yet
            filled.append(last_valid)
    return filled

def fill_interpolate(temps):
    """Fill missing values by linear interpolation."""
    filled = list(temps)  # Copy
    
    i = 0
    while i < len(filled):
        if filled[i] is None:
            # Find next non-None value
            j = i + 1
            while j < len(filled) and filled[j] is None:
                j += 1
            
            # If we have a previous and next value, interpolate
            if i > 0 and j < len(filled):
                prev_val = filled[i-1]
                next_val = filled[j]
                gap = j - i + 1
                
                # Linear interpolation
                for k in range(i, j):
                    fraction = (k - i + 1) / gap
                    filled[k] = prev_val + fraction * (next_val - prev_val)
            
            i = j
        else:
            i += 1
    
    return filled

print("Original:", temps)
print("Mean fill:", fill_with_mean_naive(temps))
print("Forward fill:", fill_forward(temps))
print("Interpolate:", fill_interpolate(temps))

    result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
    assert result == [(1, 3, 88.0)], "Should detect 3-day heat wave"
    
    print("All heat wave tests passed!")

# Step 2: Implement
def find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85):
    """
    Find heat waves in temperature data.
    
    A heat wave is 3+ consecutive days above threshold.
    
    Args:
        temps: list of daily temperatures
        threshold: temperature threshold for heat wave
        
    Returns:
        list of tuples: (start_idx, end_idx, avg_temp)
    """
    if len(temps) < 3:
        return []
    
    heat_waves = []
    in_heat_wave = False
    start_idx = None
    
    for i in range(len(temps)):
        if temps[i] > threshold:
            if not in_heat_wave:
                # Potential start of heat wave
                start_idx = i
                in_heat_wave = True
        else:
            # Below threshold
            if in_heat_wave:
                # Heat wave just ended
                end_idx = i - 1
                duration = end_idx - start_idx + 1
                
                if duration >= 3:
                    # Valid heat wave (3+ days)
                    wave_temps = temps[start_idx:end_idx+1]
                    avg_temp = sum(wave_temps) / len(wave_temps)
                    heat_waves.append((start_idx, end_idx, avg_temp))
                
                in_heat_wave = False
                start_idx = None
    
    # Check if we ended in a heat wave
    if in_heat_wave:
        end_idx = len(temps) - 1
        duration = end_idx - start_idx + 1
        if duration >= 3:
            wave_temps = temps[start_idx:end_idx+1]
            avg_temp = sum(wave_temps) / len(wave_temps)
            heat_waves.append((start_idx, end_idx, avg_temp))
    
    return heat_waves

# Step 3: Run tests
test_find_heat_waves()

# Additional validation
temps = [70, 80, 86, 88, 90, 92, 82, 75, 87, 89, 91]
result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
print(f"\nHeat waves found: {result}")
# Should find two: days 2-5 and days 8-10

All heat wave tests passed!

Heat waves found: [(2, 5, 89.0), (8, 10, 89.0)]


Instructor notes:
This is the capstone exercise demonstrating the full workflow:

Requirements first: Clear specification of what “heat wave” means
Tests before implementation: Thought through edge cases
Implementation: Careful algorithm with state tracking
Verification: Tests pass, validates correctness

Common implementation challenges:

State management (are we currently in a heat wave?)
Ending detection (what if heat wave goes to end of data?)
Duration counting (off-by-one errors)
Average calculation (need to extract the right slice)

This problem is complex enough to show:

Why planning is important
Why tests catch bugs
Why systematic thinking matters

Alternative implementation using a different approach:

def find_heat_waves_v2(temps, threshold=85):
    """Alternative implementation using boolean mask."""
    if len(temps) < 3:
        return []
    
    # Create boolean mask of hot days
    is_hot = [t > threshold for t in temps]
    
    heat_waves = []
    i = 0
    
    while i < len(is_hot):
        if is_hot[i]:
            # Start of potential heat wave
            j = i
            while j < len(is_hot) and is_hot[j]:
                j += 1
            
            # j is now first non-hot day (or end of list)
            duration = j - i
            
            if duration >= 3:
                wave_temps = temps[i:j]
                avg_temp = sum(wave_temps) / len(wave_temps)
                heat_waves.append((i, j-1, avg_temp))
            
            i = j
        else:
            i += 1
    
    return heat_waves

Discuss: Which implementation is clearer? More efficient? Easier to debug?
This demonstrates that there are multiple valid approaches. Tests help verify they all work correctly.

def normalize_temperatures(temps):
    """
    Normalize temperatures to 0-1 scale using min-max normalization.
    Formula: (value - min) / (max - min)
    
    Args:
        temps: list of temperature values
        
    Returns:
        list: normalized values (0-1 scale)
    """
    if len(temps) == 0:
        return []
    
    min_temp = min(temps)
    max_temp = max(temps)
    
    # Handle case where all values are the same
    if max_temp == min_temp:
        return [0.5] * len(temps)  # or could return all 0s or all 1s
    
    return [(t - min_temp) / (max_temp - min_temp) for t in temps]

# Test 1: Normal case
result = normalize_temperatures([0, 50, 100])
expected = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]
for i in range(len(expected)):
    assert abs(result[i] - expected[i]) < 0.01, \
        f"At index {i}: expected {expected[i]}, got {result[i]}"
print("Test 1 passed: normal case")

# Test 2: All same value
result = normalize_temperatures([10, 10, 10])
# This is a design decision: what should happen?
# We chose 0.5 for all values (middle of range)
assert all(abs(v - 0.5) < 0.01 for v in result), \
    "All same values should normalize to 0.5"
print("Test 2 passed: all same value")

# Test 3: Reverse order
result = normalize_temperatures([100, 50])
expected = [1.0, 0.0]  # 100 is still max, 50 is still min
for i in range(len(expected)):
    assert abs(result[i] - expected[i]) < 0.01, \
        f"At index {i}: expected {expected[i]}, got {result[i]}"
print("Test 3 passed: reverse order")

Test 1 passed: normal case
Test 2 passed: all same value
Test 3 passed: reverse order


Instructor notes:
This exercise introduces an important concept: design decisions. When all values are the same, what should normalization return? There are multiple valid answers:

All 0s (min value)
All 0.5s (middle)
All 1s (max value)
Raise an error
Return original values

The key is that students make a choice and document it. This is a great discussion point: “There’s no single ‘right’ answer, but you must handle this case somehow.”
Common mistakes:

Not handling the all-same-value case (division by zero)
Assuming input is sorted
Not using floating-point comparison tolerance

Teaching moment: Ask students to defend their choice for the all-same-value case.

def calculate_median_fixed(values):
    """
    Calculate median of values.
    
    Args:
        values: list of numeric values
        
    Returns:
        float: median value, or None if empty
    """
    if len(values) == 0:
        return None
    
    sorted_values = sorted(values)
    n = len(sorted_values)
    middle = n // 2  # Integer division!
    
    if n % 2 == 1:
        # Odd length: return middle element
        return sorted_values[middle]
    else:
        # Even length: return average of two middle elements
        return (sorted_values[middle - 1] + sorted_values[middle]) / 2

# Test cases

result = calculate_median_fixed(temps)
assert result == 75, f"Expected 75, got {result}"
print("Test passed: odd length")

temps = [68, 72, 80, 85]
result = calculate_median_fixed(temps)
assert result == 76.0, f"Expected 76.0, got {result}"
print("Test passed: even length")

result = calculate_median_fixed([])
assert result is None, f"Expected None, got {result}"
print("Test passed: empty list")

Test passed: odd length
Test passed: even length
Test passed: empty list


Instructor notes:
Key bug fixes:

Used // (integer division) instead of / (float division)
Added empty list check
Handled even-length lists correctly (average of two middle elements)

Students often miss the even-length case because they test only with odd-length lists. This reinforces the importance of testing multiple scenarios.
Common mistakes:

Forgetting that sorted() returns a new list (doesn’t modify original)
Not handling even-length lists at all
Off-by-one errors in indexing

Teaching moment: Have students trace through execution manually with both odd and even length lists.

def get_temperature_range_fixed(temps):
    """
    Get range of temperatures (max - min).
    
    Args:
        temps: list of temperature values
        
    Returns:
        float: max - min, or None if empty
    """
    if len(temps) == 0:
        return None
    
    min_temp = temps[0]
    max_temp = temps[0]
    
    # Fix: Check ALL elements
    for i in range(len(temps)):
        if temps[i] < min_temp:
            min_temp = temps[i]
        if temps[i] > max_temp:
            max_temp = temps[i]
    
    return max_temp - min_temp

# Test with last value being important
temps = [72, 75, 68, 90]
result = get_temperature_range_fixed(temps)
assert result == 22, f"Expected 22, got {result}"
print("Test passed: last value is max")

# Test with first value being important
temps = [90, 75, 68, 72]
result = get_temperature_range_fixed(temps)
assert result == 22, f"Expected 22, got {result}"
print("Test passed: first value is max")

Test passed: last value is max
Test passed: first value is max


Instructor notes:
The bug was range(len(temps) - 1) which stops one element too early. This is a classic off-by-one error.
Alternative (more Pythonic) solutions:

# Using built-in functions
def get_temperature_range_v2(temps):
    if len(temps) == 0:
        return None
    return max(temps) - min(temps)

# Using direct iteration (no indices)
def get_temperature_range_v3(temps):
    if len(temps) == 0:
        return None
    min_temp = temps[0]
    max_temp = temps[0]
    for temp in temps:  # Simpler!
        if temp < min_temp:
            min_temp = temp
        if temp > max_temp:
            max_temp = temp
    return max_temp - min_temp

Discuss: Which is clearest? Most Pythonic? Easiest to debug?
Teaching tip: Off-by-one errors are extremely common. Always check loop bounds carefully.

def calculate_total_rainfall_robust(daily_rain):
    """
    Sum daily rainfall, handling type mismatches gracefully.
    
    Args:
        daily_rain: list of rainfall measurements (should be numeric)
        
    Returns:
        float: total rainfall, skipping invalid values
    """
    total = 0
    for i, rain in enumerate(daily_rain):
        # Handle numeric types directly
        if isinstance(rain, (int, float)):
            total += rain
        # Try to convert strings
        elif isinstance(rain, str):
            try:
                converted = float(rain)
                total += converted
            except ValueError:
                print(f"Warning: Skipping invalid string at index {i}: '{rain}'")
        # Skip None
        elif rain is None:
            print(f"Warning: Skipping None at index {i}")
        # Unknown types
        else:
            print(f"Warning: Skipping unknown type at index {i}: {type(rain)}")
    
    return total

# Test with messy data

print(f"Total: {result}")
# Should print warnings for "invalid" and None
# Should handle string "0.8" successfully
# Expected: 0.5 + 0.0 + 1.2 + 0.8 + 0.3 = 2.8
assert abs(result - 2.8) < 0.01, f"Expected 2.8, got {result}"
print("Test passed!")

Warning: Skipping None at index 6
Total: 2.8
Test passed!


Instructor notes:
This exercise teaches defensive programming – handling unexpected input gracefully. Key concepts:

Type checking with isinstance()
Try-except for conversion
Informative warning messages
Continuing despite errors rather than crashing

Design decisions students must make:

Should invalid values be skipped or cause an error?
Should we log warnings or fail silently?
Should we track how many values were skipped?

Alternative approach (fail fast):

def calculate_total_rainfall_strict(daily_rain):
    """Strict version that raises errors on invalid input."""
    total = 0
    for i, rain in enumerate(daily_rain):
        if not isinstance(rain, (int, float)):
            raise TypeError(f"Invalid type at index {i}: {type(rain)}")
        total += rain
    return total

Discuss: When should we be lenient vs strict? Data cleaning often requires leniency; financial calculations require strictness.

def calculate_std_dev(values):
    """Calculate standard deviation (sample)."""
    if len(values) == 0:
        return None
    if len(values) == 1:
        return 0.0  # Single value has no variation
    
    n = len(values)
    mean = sum(values) / n
    
    # Use n-1 for sample standard deviation
    variance = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in values) / (n - 1)
    return variance ** 0.5

def remove_outliers(values, z_threshold=2):
    """Remove outliers beyond z_threshold standard deviations."""
    if len(values) < 2:
        return values  # Can't calculate std dev with < 2 values
    
    mean = sum(values) / len(values)
    std_dev = calculate_std_dev(values)
    
    if std_dev == 0:
        # All values are the same -- no outliers
        return values
    
    return [x for x in values if abs(x - mean) <= z_threshold * std_dev]

# Tests to reveal bugs/edge cases:

# Test 1: Normal case

result = remove_outliers(data)

print("Test 2 passed: all same values")

print("Test 3 passed: single value")

result = remove_outliers(data, z_threshold=0.5)
# With strict threshold, might remove everything!
print(f"Test 4: All outliers case returned {result}")
# This is actually a valid result -- all were outliers

def is_valid_temperature_reading(temp, unit):
    """
    Validate temperature reading.
    
    Args:
        temp: numeric temperature value
        unit: string, either "C" or "F"
        
    Returns:
        bool: True if reading is physically plausible
    """
    if unit == "C":
        return -273.15 <= temp <= 100
    elif unit == "F":
        return -459.67 <= temp <= 212
    else:
        return False

# AI might suggest these basic tests:
def test_temperature_reading_ai_version():
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(25, "C") == True
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(75, "F") == True
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(-300, "C") == False
    print("AI tests passed")

# Additional tests that AI missed:
def test_temperature_reading_comprehensive():
    # Boundary values (exactly at limits)
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(-273.15, "C") == True
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(100, "C") == True
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(-459.67, "F") == True
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(212, "F") == True
    
    # Just beyond boundaries
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(-273.16, "C") == False
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(100.01, "C") == False
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(-459.68, "F") == False
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(212.01, "F") == False
    
    # Invalid units
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(25, "K") == False
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(25, "celsius") == False
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(25, "") == False
    
    # Case sensitivity
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(25, "c") == False
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(75, "f") == False
    
    # Extreme but valid values
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(0, "C") == True
    assert is_valid_temperature_reading(32, "F") == True
    
    # Type mismatches (if we want to be thorough)
    # Note: These might raise TypeErrors depending on implementation
    try:
        result = is_valid_temperature_reading("25", "C")
        # If it doesn't raise an error, it should return False
        assert result == False
    except TypeError:
        # Or it might raise an error, which is also acceptable
        pass
    
    print("Comprehensive tests passed!")

test_temperature_reading_ai_version()
test_temperature_reading_comprehensive()

AI tests passed
Comprehensive tests passed!


Instructor notes:
This exercise teaches comprehensive testing. AI often suggests obvious tests but misses:

Boundary values (exactly at limits)
Just-beyond-boundary values
Invalid input types
Case sensitivity
Edge cases specific to domain

Students should learn to ask:

What are the boundaries?
What happens just inside/outside boundaries?
What invalid inputs might occur?
What assumptions does the code make?

Teaching tip: Have students brainstorm test cases before looking at solution. List them on the board, then implement.

def moving_average_corrected(values, window_size):
    """
    Calculate moving average, excluding incomplete windows.
    
    Args:
        values: list of numeric values
        window_size: size of moving window (must be >= 1)
        
    Returns:
        list: moving averages (length may be shorter than input)
    """
    # Handle edge cases
    if window_size < 1:
        raise ValueError("window_size must be >= 1")
    
    if len(values) < window_size:
        return []
    
    # Special case: window_size == 1
    if window_size == 1:
        return list(values)  # Return copy
    
    # Calculate moving averages for complete windows only
    result = []
    for i in range(len(values) - window_size + 1):
        window = values[i:i+window_size]
        avg = sum(window) / window_size
        result.append(avg)
    
    return result

# Test cases
temps = [70, 75, 80, 85, 90]

# Normal case: window_size = 3
ma = moving_average_corrected(temps, window_size=3)
expected = [75.0, 80.0, 85.0]
assert ma == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {ma}"
print("Test passed: window_size=3")

# Edge case: window_size > len(values)
ma = moving_average_corrected([1, 2, 3], 5)
assert ma == [], "Should return empty list"
print("Test passed: window too large")

# Edge case: window_size = 1
ma = moving_average_corrected([1, 2, 3], 1)
assert ma == [1, 2, 3], "window_size=1 should return original"
print("Test passed: window_size=1")

# Edge case: window_size = len(values)
ma = moving_average_corrected([1, 2, 3], 3)
assert ma == [2.0], "Should return single value"
print("Test passed: window equals length")

Test passed: window_size=3
Test passed: window too large
Test passed: window_size=1
Test passed: window equals length


Instructor notes:
Key fixes:

Only compute averages for complete windows
Handle window_size > len(values)
Handle window_size == 1
Correct loop bounds: range(len(values) - window_size + 1)

The loop bound formula is tricky. Have students work it out:

If values has 5 elements and window_size is 3
Valid starting positions: 0, 1, 2 (produces 3 windows)
So we need: range(5 - 3 + 1) = range(3) = [0, 1, 2] ✓

Teaching moment: This is mathematical reasoning applied to programming. Drawing diagrams helps:
values:  [70, 75, 80, 85, 90]
          ↑-window-↑             position 0: [70,75,80] -> 75.0
             ↑-window-↑          position 1: [75,80,85] -> 80.0
                ↑-window-↑       position 2: [80,85,90] -> 85.0

def fill_with_mean_naive(temps):
    """Fill missing values with mean of valid values."""
    valid_temps = [t for t in temps if t is not None]
    if len(valid_temps) == 0:
        return temps  # All None, can't compute mean
    mean_temp = sum(valid_temps) / len(valid_temps)
    return [t if t is not None else mean_temp for t in temps]

def fill_forward(temps):
    """Fill missing values by carrying forward last valid value."""
    filled = []
    last_valid = None
    for temp in temps:
        if temp is not None:
            filled.append(temp)
            last_valid = temp
        else:
            # Use last valid value, or None if we haven't seen one yet
            filled.append(last_valid)
    return filled

def fill_interpolate(temps):
    """Fill missing values by linear interpolation."""
    filled = list(temps)  # Copy
    
    i = 0
    while i < len(filled):
        if filled[i] is None:
            # Find next non-None value
            j = i + 1
            while j < len(filled) and filled[j] is None:
                j += 1
            
            # If we have a previous and next value, interpolate
            if i > 0 and j < len(filled):
                prev_val = filled[i-1]
                next_val = filled[j]
                gap = j - i + 1
                
                # Linear interpolation
                for k in range(i, j):
                    fraction = (k - i + 1) / gap
                    filled[k] = prev_val + fraction * (next_val - prev_val)
            
            i = j
        else:
            i += 1
    
    return filled

# Compare methods on same data
temps = [70, None, None, 85, None, 90]

print("Original:", temps)
print("Mean fill:", fill_with_mean_naive(temps))
print("Forward fill:", fill_forward(temps))
print("Interpolate:", fill_interpolate(temps))

# Which is most appropriate for temperature data?
"""
Analysis:

Mean fill: [70, 81.67, 81.67, 85, 81.67, 90]
- Pros: Simple, preserves overall average
- Cons: Ignores temporal patterns, creates flat spots

Forward fill: [70, 70, 70, 85, 85, 90]
- Pros: Maintains temporal continuity
- Cons: Can extend incorrect values, not suitable for trends

Interpolate: [70, 75, 80, 85, 87.5, 90]
- Pros: Smooth, reasonable for gradual changes
- Cons: Assumes linear change, doesn't capture actual variation

For temperature data, interpolation is often best because:
1. Temperature changes gradually over time
2. Interpolation maintains smooth transitions
3. Doesn't create artificial flat spots

However, for large gaps, forward fill might be more conservative
(doesn't assume we know the pattern).

The "right" choice depends on:
- Size of gaps (interpolation unreliable for large gaps)
- Nature of the data (gradual vs sudden changes)
- Purpose of analysis (summary stats vs time series)
"""

Original: [70, None, None, 85, None, 90]
Mean fill: [70, 81.66666666666667, 81.66666666666667, 85, 81.66666666666667, 90]
Forward fill: [70, 70, 70, 85, 85, 90]
Interpolate: [70, 75.0, 80.0, 85, 87.5, 90]


'\nAnalysis:\n\nMean fill: [70, 81.67, 81.67, 85, 81.67, 90]\n- Pros: Simple, preserves overall average\n- Cons: Ignores temporal patterns, creates flat spots\n\nForward fill: [70, 70, 70, 85, 85, 90]\n- Pros: Maintains temporal continuity\n- Cons: Can extend incorrect values, not suitable for trends\n\nInterpolate: [70, 75, 80, 85, 87.5, 90]\n- Pros: Smooth, reasonable for gradual changes\n- Cons: Assumes linear change, doesn\'t capture actual variation\n\nFor temperature data, interpolation is often best because:\n1. Temperature changes gradually over time\n2. Interpolation maintains smooth transitions\n3. Doesn\'t create artificial flat spots\n\nHowever, for large gaps, forward fill might be more conservative\n(doesn\'t assume we know the pattern).\n\nThe "right" choice depends on:\n- Size of gaps (interpolation unreliable for large gaps)\n- Nature of the data (gradual vs sudden changes)\n- Purpose of analysis (summary stats vs time series)\n'


Instructor notes:
This is an excellent discussion exercise. There is no single “right” answer – the choice depends on context.
Key teaching points:

Different imputation methods make different assumptions
The method should match your data’s characteristics
Document which method you chose and why
Consider impact on downstream analysis

Students should understand:

Mean fill: Good for summary statistics, bad for time series
Forward fill: Good for maintaining last known state, bad for trends
Interpolation: Good for gradual changes, bad for volatile data
In practice, you might use different methods for different variables

Real-world consideration: Sometimes the best choice is to NOT fill missing values and instead do analysis that accounts for missingness.

text:
# Step 1: Write requirements and tests FIRST
def test_find_heat_waves():
    """Test heat wave detection."""
    
    # Test 1: Basic heat wave (3 consecutive days)
    temps = [70, 80, 86, 88, 90, 82, 75]
    result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
    assert result == [(2, 4, 88.0)], f"Expected [(2, 4, 88.0)], got {result}"
    
    # Test 2: No heat wave
    temps = [70, 75, 80, 82, 84]
    result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
    assert result == [], "No heat wave should be found"
    
    # Test 3: Entire period is heat wave
    temps = [90, 92, 91, 93]
    result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
    assert len(result) == 1 and result[0][0] == 0 and result[0][1] == 3
    
    # Test 4: Multiple heat waves
    temps = [86, 88, 90, 70, 75, 87, 89, 91, 93]
    result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
    assert len(result) == 2, "Should find two separate heat waves"
    
    # Test 5: Heat wave exactly 3 days
    temps = [70, 86, 88, 90, 70]
    result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
    assert result == [(1, 3, 88.0)], "Should detect 3-day heat wave"
    
    print("All heat wave tests passed!")

# Step 2: Implement
def find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85):
    """
    Find heat waves in temperature data.
    
    A heat wave is 3+ consecutive days above threshold.
    
    Args:
        temps: list of daily temperatures
        threshold: temperature threshold for heat wave
        
    Returns:
        list of tuples: (start_idx, end_idx, avg_temp)
    """
    if len(temps) < 3:
        return []
    
    heat_waves = []
    in_heat_wave = False
    start_idx = None
    
    for i in range(len(temps)):
        if temps[i] > threshold:
            if not in_heat_wave:
                # Potential start of heat wave
                start_idx = i
                in_heat_wave = True
        else:
            # Below threshold
            if in_heat_wave:
                # Heat wave just ended
                end_idx = i - 1
                duration = end_idx - start_idx + 1
                
                if duration >= 3:
                    # Valid heat wave (3+ days)
                    wave_temps = temps[start_idx:end_idx+1]
                    avg_temp = sum(wave_temps) / len(wave_temps)
                    heat_waves.append((start_idx, end_idx, avg_temp))
                
                in_heat_wave = False
                start_idx = None
    
    # Check if we ended in a heat wave
    if in_heat_wave:
        end_idx = len(temps) - 1
        duration = end_idx - start_idx + 1
        if duration >= 3:
            wave_temps = temps[start_idx:end_idx+1]
            avg_temp = sum(wave_temps) / len(wave_temps)
            heat_waves.append((start_idx, end_idx, avg_temp))
    
    return heat_waves

# Step 3: Run tests
test_find_heat_waves()

# Additional validation
temps = [70, 80, 86, 88, 90, 92, 82, 75, 87, 89, 91]
result = find_heat_waves(temps, threshold=85)
print(f"\nHeat waves found: {result}")
# Should find two: days 2-5 and days 8-10

All heat wave tests passed!

Heat waves found: [(2, 5, 89.0), (8, 10, 89.0)]


Instructor notes:
This is the capstone exercise demonstrating the full workflow:

Requirements first: Clear specification of what “heat wave” means
Tests before implementation: Thought through edge cases
Implementation: Careful algorithm with state tracking
Verification: Tests pass, validates correctness

Common implementation challenges:

State management (are we currently in a heat wave?)
Ending detection (what if heat wave goes to end of data?)
Duration counting (off-by-one errors)
Average calculation (need to extract the right slice)

This problem is complex enough to show:

Why planning is important
Why tests catch bugs
Why systematic thinking matters

Alternative implementation using a different approach:

def find_heat_waves_v2(temps, threshold=85):
    """Alternative implementation using boolean mask."""
    if len(temps) < 3:
        return []
    
    # Create boolean mask of hot days
    is_hot = [t > threshold for t in temps]
    
    heat_waves = []
    i = 0
    
    while i < len(is_hot):
        if is_hot[i]:
            # Start of potential heat wave
            j = i
            while j < len(is_hot) and is_hot[j]:
                j += 1
            
            # j is now first non-hot day (or end of list)
            duration = j - i
            
            if duration >= 3:
                wave_temps = temps[i:j]
                avg_temp = sum(wave_temps) / len(wave_temps)
                heat_waves.append((i, j-1, avg_temp))
            
            i = j
        else:
            i += 1
    
    return heat_waves

Discuss: Which implementation is clearer? More efficient? Easier to debug?
This demonstrates that there are multiple valid approaches. Tests help verify they all work correctly.

title: Lecture 6: Testing, Debugging, and AI-Assisted Programming
text:
Common Student Difficulties

Resistance to testing: Students want to just write code and move on. They don’t see value until they experience catching a bug with tests.
Teaching strategy: Show examples of subtle bugs that tests catch. Emphasize that “it seems to work” ≠ “it works correctly”
Forgetting edge cases: Students test only the happy path.
Teaching strategy: Always ask “What could go wrong?” Make edge case thinking a habit.
Not reading error messages carefully: Students see an error and give up.
Teaching strategy: Teach systematic error interpretation. Model reading error messages aloud.
Over-trust of AI: Students assume AI-generated code is correct.
Teaching strategy: Show examples of plausible but buggy AI code. Emphasize verification.
Print debugging without strategy: Students add print() randomly instead of systematically.
Teaching strategy: Teach strategic print placement: inputs, intermediate values, outputs, loop progress.
Not understanding what “correct” means: Students can’t write tests because they don’t know what the function should do.
Teaching strategy: Start by writing specifications in plain English. Then translate to tests.
Comparing floats with ==: Students don’t understand floating-point precision.
Teaching strategy: Show examples where 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 in floating-point. Teach tolerance-based comparison.
Writing tests after code: Students view testing as verification after completion rather than during development.
Teaching strategy: Demonstrate test-driven development. Show how tests clarify requirements.

title: Lecture 6: Testing, Debugging, and AI-Assisted Programming
text:
Teaching Tips

Live debugging: When teaching debugging, intentionally write buggy code and debug it live in class. Talk through your reasoning process.
Pair testing: Have students work in pairs – one writes function, other writes tests. Then switch.
Test coverage game: Give students a function and challenge them to write tests that cover all branches.
Bug hunt: Give students intentionally buggy code. First student to find the bug (with a test) wins.
AI code review: Give students AI-generated code. Have them critique it, find bugs, write tests.
Debugging checklist: Provide systematic checklist:

What did I expect?
What actually happened?
What are my assumptions?
What does the error message say?
What do intermediate values show?

Test-first challenge: Require tests before implementation for at least one exercise.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
What Operations Do We Need?
To answer these questions computationally, we need to:

Store the observations in a structured way
Access individual observations
Process each observation in turn
Compare observations
Make decisions based on conditions
Accumulate results

This lecture will show you how to perform each of these operations.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Control Flow: The Common Pattern
All control flow structures in Python follow the same pattern:
[KEYWORD] [CONDITION]:
    [INDENTED STATEMENT(S)]
    [MORE INDENTED STATEMENTS...]
[UNINDENTED CODE CONTINUES HERE]
Key elements:

Keyword tells Python what kind of control structure
Condition (or iteration variable) determines when/how it executes
Colon (:) signals the start of the code block
Indentation (4 spaces) defines what’s inside the block
Unindenting ends the block


The Three Main Control Structures
# FOR LOOP: Iterate through a collection
for item in collection:
    # Do something with item
    print(item)

# WHILE LOOP: Repeat while condition is true  
while condition_is_true:
    # Do something
    # Update something to eventually make condition false
    
# IF/ELIF/ELSE: Conditional execution
if condition1:
    # Do this if condition1 is true
elif condition2:
    # Do this if condition1 is false but condition2 is true
else:
    # Do this if all conditions are false
Notice: Same pattern every time—keyword, condition/variable, colon, indent!

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Data Structures: Know Your Delimiters
Each data structure uses different brackets:









Structure
Delimiter
Example
When to Use




List
[...]
[1, 2, 3]
Ordered sequence, can modify


Tuple
(...)
(1, 2, 3)
Ordered sequence, cannot modify


Set
{...}
{1, 2, 3}
Unique values, no order


Dict
{k:v, ...}
{"a": 1, "b": 2}
Key-value pairs for lookup




Quick Reference
# LIST: Square brackets, ordered, mutable
temps = [15.2, 17.1, 14.8]
temps[0]          # Access: 15.2
temps.append(19)  # Modify: add to end

# TUPLE: Parentheses, ordered, immutable  
point = (10, 20)
point[0]          # Access: 10
# point[0] = 15   # ERROR: can't modify

# SET: Curly braces, unique values, no order
unique = {1, 2, 3, 2, 1}  # Becomes {1, 2, 3}
2 in unique               # Fast membership test: True

# DICT: Curly braces with colons, key-value pairs
counts = {"a": 5, "b": 3}
counts["a"]               # Access by key: 5
counts["c"] = 7           # Add new key-value pair






TipWhen You See…




Square brackets [] → Working with a list (ordered, can change)
Parentheses () → Working with a tuple (ordered, cannot change)

Curly braces {} → Working with a set (unique items) or dict (has colons)
Keyword + colon : + indent → Starting a control flow block

Whitespace matters in Python! Keep your indentation consistent (4 spaces is standard).


Now let’s put these patterns to use.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Exercise 1.1: Representing the Observations
Question: How should we represent a collection of temperature measurements in Python?

What We Need
We need a representation that:

preserves the order of observations (day 1, day 2, etc.)
allows us to access individual temperatures
can grow or shrink if needed



Python Lists
Python provides a list for exactly this purpose:

temperatures = [15.2, 17.1, 14.8, 19.3, 16.5, 18.2, 14.1, 20.5]

A list:

is ordered - elements have positions
is mutable - we can change it
uses square brackets []

We can access individual elements using indexing:

temperatures[0]  # First temperature

15.2



temperatures[3]  # Fourth temperature

19.3


Python uses zero-based indexing: the first element is at position 0.
Temperatures:  [15.2, 17.1, 14.8, 19.3, 16.5, 18.2, 14.1, 20.5]
Indices:         0     1     2     3     4     5     6     7
We can also index from the end:

temperatures[-1]  # Last temperature

20.5



temperatures[-2]  # Second-to-last temperature

14.1




Slicing
We can extract portions using slicing:

temperatures[0:3]  # First three temperatures

[15.2, 17.1, 14.8]



temperatures[2:5]  # Days 3-5

[14.8, 19.3, 16.5]


The general form is list[start:stop]. The start is included, but stop is excluded.

temperatures[:4]  # First four (omit start → begins at 0)

[15.2, 17.1, 14.8, 19.3]



temperatures[4:]  # From day 5 onward (omit stop → goes to end)

[16.5, 18.2, 14.1, 20.5]




Basic List Operations
How many observations do we have?

len(temperatures)

8


What if we collect a new measurement?

temperatures.append(17.8)
temperatures

[15.2, 17.1, 14.8, 19.3, 16.5, 18.2, 14.1, 20.5, 17.8]








NoteLists Are Mutable



Unlike strings (which we’ll see later), lists can be modified after creation. This is useful when building up a collection of results.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Exercise 1.2: Finding the Maximum Temperature
Question: How can we determine the highest temperature in our collection?

Algorithm Design
Before writing code, let’s design the algorithm in plain English:

Start by assuming the first temperature is the maximum
Look at each remaining temperature
If we find a temperature higher than our current maximum, update the maximum
After examining all temperatures, return the maximum

Pause: Read through this algorithm. Does it make sense? Can you think of any problems with it?


Implementation: The for Loop
To “look at each remaining temperature,” we need iteration. Python’s for loop does exactly this:

temperatures = [15.2, 17.1, 14.8, 19.3, 16.5, 18.2, 14.1, 20.5]

current_max = temperatures[0]

for temp in temperatures[1:]:
    if temp > current_max:
        current_max = temp

print(f"Maximum temperature: {current_max}°C")

Maximum temperature: 20.5°C




Understanding the Loop
Let’s trace through the first few iterations:
Initial: current_max = 15.2

Iteration 1: temp = 17.1
  17.1 > 15.2? Yes → current_max = 17.1

Iteration 2: temp = 14.8
  14.8 > 17.1? No → current_max stays 17.1

Iteration 3: temp = 19.3
  19.3 > 17.1? Yes → current_max = 19.3

... and so on
The loop repeats the comparison for each temperature. This is why we need iteration: we’re performing the same operation multiple times.


The if Statement
The line:
if temp > current_max:
    current_max = temp
demonstrates conditional execution. The update only happens when the condition is true.


Validation
How do we know our answer is correct?

# Python has a built-in max() function
max(temperatures)

20.5


Our algorithm produces the same result. This is a simple example of validation: checking our implementation against a known answer or alternative method.

section: Exercise 1.3: Counting Days Above a Threshold
text:
Exercise 1.3: Counting Days Above a Threshold
Question: On how many days did the temperature exceed 17°C?

Algorithm Design

Start with a count of zero
Examine each temperature
If the temperature exceeds the threshold, increase the count
Return the final count



Implementation

temperatures = [15.2, 17.1, 14.8, 19.3, 16.5, 18.2, 14.1, 20.5]
threshold = 17.0

count = 0

for temp in temperatures:
    if temp > threshold:
        count += 1

print(f"Days above {threshold}°C: {count}")

Days above 17.0°C: 4


###Accumulators
The variable count is an accumulator. It maintains state across iterations:
Before loop: count = 0

After temp = 15.2: count = 0  (not above threshold)
After temp = 17.1: count = 1  (above threshold)
After temp = 14.8: count = 1  (not above threshold)
After temp = 19.3: count = 2  (above threshold)
...
This pattern—initialize → iterate → update → return—appears frequently in computational problems.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Exercise 1.4: Computing Summary Statistics
Question: What was the average temperature?

Algorithm Design

Start with a sum of zero
Add each temperature to the sum
Divide by the number of temperatures



Implementation

temperatures = [15.2, 17.1, 14.8, 19.3, 16.5, 18.2, 14.1, 20.5]

total = 0
count = 0

for temp in temperatures:
    total += temp
    count += 1

average = total / count

print(f"Average temperature: {average:.1f}°C")

Average temperature: 17.0°C




Multiple Accumulators
Notice we’re maintaining two pieces of state:

total - the running sum
count - the number of observations



Edge Cases
Question: What happens if the list is empty?

total = 0
count = 0

for temp in temperatures:
    total += temp
    count += 1

average = total / count  # Division by zero!
